Osteoarthritis
NRBS 4210
Professor Carissa Coccimiglio DNP , FNP-BC
By: Lesly Theramen Junior Jean Joseph, Aniqa Mayesha, Lakota Ogiura, 
Xinlian Pan, Tamika Simeon, Connie Tang, Rachel Zila

Osteoarthritis Overview
Non-modifiable:
● Advanced age, especially over age 60
● Female sex, especially after age 55
● Family history
● Inherited metabolic or congenital bone 
deformities
Modifiable:
● Obesity
● Repetitive joint stress & muscle weakness
● Smoking
● Joint trauma (previous injury)
● Physically demanding occupation (such as 
construction/agriculture)
● Participation in athletics
Risk Factors
(Hinkle et al., 2025)
Background
● OA is the most common non-inflammatory 
degenerative disorder of the joints
○ Primary (idiopathic): Develops 
without a known cause or previous 
injury
○ Secondary: Develops due to a 
previous injury or another condition, 
such as RA
● OA can begin in your 30s, with symptoms 
becoming more common by your 50s and 
60s

Prevention, Health Promotion, and Early 
Detection 
Prevention & Health Promotion
● Make lifestyle changes if needed to 
maintain a healthy weight
● Engage in low-impact exercise (swimming, 
biking, yoga); avoid high-impact sports
● Strength training in the lower extremities
● Wear supportive gear (insoles, properly 
fitting shoes, braces, splints, canes) to distribute 
stress and prevent falls from movement
● Quit smoking to prevent loss of cartilage
● Physical & occupational therapy to 
reduce pain and increase ROM
● Engage in rest after activity; use heat for 
stiffness and ice for inflammation
● Integrative therapies: massage, yoga, 
special diets, acupuncture
Key Considerations for Early 
Detection
● Osteoarthritis involves more than cartilage loss; it 
can also affect the bones, ligaments, menisci, 
joint lining and surrounding tissues
● Since osteoarthritis progresses slowly over 
approximately 10 to 20 years, identifying early 
signs is essential
● There is no universal age of OA screening. 
Evaluation is performed after symptoms appear
● Early detection and diagnosis may be made via 
knee pain, minimal changes on X-rays and 
structural abnormalities detected through 
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
● Unlike X-rays, MRI can visualize multiple joint 
tissues, making it a valuable tool for identifying 
early damage and guiding appropriate treatment 
strategies
(Hinkle et al., 2025)

Symptoms
● Pain, stiffness, and functional impairment (reduced ROM)
● Joint pain worsens with activity and improves with rest
● Some experience morning stiffness (lasts less than 30 minutes)
● Unilateral – symptoms may affect one side or joint more than the other, especially in early 
disease 
Onset & Progression
● Insidious onset, progressing over several years
Commonly Affected Joints
● Primarily affects weight-bearing joints
○ Hips, knees, cervical and lumbar spine
● May occur in finger joints
○ Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints
Physical Findings
● Bony enlargement of DIP (Heberden’s nodes) and PIP (Bouchard’s nodes)
● Crepitus (grating sensation) may be palpated if the joint is hot to touch, visibly bright red, 
severely swollen, and if you have a fever
○ Especially in the knee
● Joint effusion is usually mild from overuse
● No systemic manifestations
Clinical Manifestations
(Hinkle et al., 2025)

Diagnostic Tests
● OA is primarily diagnosed from the client’s history and joint examination 
● Clinical diagnosis can be established with findings such as:
○ Reduced range of motion
○ Morning stiffness
○ Crepitus
○ Bony enlargement 
● Blood tests such as ESR/CRP or rheumatoid factor, imaging of joints, and 
additional tests are used to rule out autoimmune or other inflammatory causes of 
the pain, when diagnosis is uncertain or other conditions are suspected 
● X-rays usually show the following 
○ Narrowing of the joint space
○ Osteophyte formation
○ Dense, thickened subchondral bone 
○ Abnormal X-ray does not exclude early OA
● MRIs are usually unnecessary for typical OA, but the provider may order when X-
ray does not explain the symptoms 
● Arthrocentesis (joint aspiration) is used for unexplained swelling or a suddenly 
hot painful joint. The joint fluid is tested for crystals, cell count, and cultured to 
rule out gout and infections 
(Hinkle et al., 2025)
(Katz et al., 2021)

Nursing Responsibilities During 
Diagnostics
● Explain the interview
● Review medication list
● Provide privacy
● Ask about pain (PQRST): 
history of morning stiffness 
and duration, difficulties 
doing daily activities, 
injuries, use of assistive 
devices
● Assess ROM, gait, crepitus
● Assess for swelling, 
tenderness, warmth, bony 
enlargement
● Document findings
● Verify patient’s identity 
and orders
● Educate and explain the 
procedures 
● Check understanding
● Position the client 
comfortably and support 
safe transfers 
● Remove objects on joints
● Screen for implants and 
metal
● Assess and reassure for 
claustrophobia 
● Ensure hearing protection
● Explain the procedure
● Review allergies and bleeding 
risks
● Verify patient’s identity and 
orders
● Verify for provider’s consent in 
arthrocentesis
● Explain local anesthesia and 
joint fluid removal 
● Use of aseptic techniques
● Label specimens
● Apply dressing,  monitor and 
assess for pain and bleeding
● Teach patient to report 
redness, fever, increasing pain, 
drainage
History and Physical X-ray and MRI Blood tests and Arthrocentesis
(Hinkle et al., 2025)
(Pedrosa et al., 2025)

Medical Management
Goal: Decrease pain and stiffness and maintain or improve joint mobility.
Nonpharmacologic Management
● Exercise: Aerobic exercise and strength training to improve mobility and reduce pain
● Weight Management: Reduce stress on affected joints
● Physical Therapy & Assistive Devices: Improve joint function and reduce joint 
stress (e.g., canes, braces)
Pharmacologic Management
● Based on the patient’s needs, disease stage, and risk of side effects
● Acetaminophen: Initial pain relief for most patients
● NSAIDs / COX-2 Inhibitors: Pain relief; use cautiously due to cardiovascular and GI 
risks. PPIs may help reduce GI complications
● Topical Analgesics: Topical NSAIDs or methyl salicylate for localized pain
● Intra-articular Corticosteroids Injection: Provide short-term pain relief. Repeated 
injections are often limited to up to 3 times per year per joint due to concerns about 
potential cartilage loss
● Tramadol / Opioids: Used for pain refractory to first-line therapies
Surgical Intervention 
● Arthroplasty: Joint replacement may be considered for severe OA when conservative 
treatments fail to relieve pain and improve function (Hinkle et al., 2025)
(Guermazi et al., 2023)

Medication Management & Nursing 
Responsibilities 
● Administer prescribed analgesics and anti-inflammatory medications after assessing OLDCARTS. 
Re-evaluate 30-60 minutes after administration for effectiveness.
○ Acetaminophen: Max dose is 4,000 mg per 24 hours. Assess renal and hepatic function 
if long-term use is expected. Monitor for hepatotoxicity (RUQ pain, jaundice, N/V, anorexia). 
Avoid alcohol and other hepatotoxic medications. Antidote: N-acetylcysteine
○ NSAIDs: Check for PUD and Hx of GI bleeds. Monitor for black, tarry stool and coffee-
ground emesis. Assess renal and hepatic function. Monitor CBC and platelet count. D/c 1 
week prior to surgery. Should be given with food to reduce GI irritation 
○ COX-2 Inhibitors: Assess for sulfonamide allergies. Assess renal and hepatic function. 
Check cardiac Hx - contraindicated in patients who have active heart disease, Hx of stroke, 
recent CABG. Monitor BP and edema due to salt and fluid retention. Monitor for rash and GI 
bleeding 
○ Intra-articular Corticosteroids Injection: Assess medical history (diabetes) and 
monitor for blood glucose spikes. Assess if they are taking blood thinners. Screen for 
infection. Maintain sterile technique and proper position during procedure. Monitor for 
infection post-procedure. Use cool compress for first 48 hours
○ Tramadol / Opioids: Assess respiratory status, BP, HR. Monitor for urinary retention and 
constipation. Encourage fluids and high fiber. Fall precautions 
(Hinkle et al., 2025)
(Richard et al., 2023)

Nursing Interventions
Nursing Priorities for Arthroplasty
● Prevent blood loss: pre-op assessment, treat anemia with epoetin alfa or 
iron supplements, intraoperative red blood cell salvage systems, pneumatic 
tourniquets, d/c medication that alter clotting a week before
● Prevent VTE – DVT & PE Inpatient: Standardized scoring (Padua 
Prediction or Caprini Score), LMWH, unfractionated heparin, DOACs, aspirin, 
neurovascular assessment, sequential compression device, compression 
socks, early ambulation, in-bed exercises, hydration, evaluate every 24-48 
hours
● Prevent infection: postpone procedure if infection presents 2-4 weeks 
prior, use antiseptic soap, prophylactic antibiotics, monitor wound drainage 
for excessive or foul-smelling drainage 
● Hip considerations: position supine with HOB slightly elevated with the 
affected leg in a neutral position and abducted 
● Assess for dislocation:  increased pain at the surgical site, swelling, 
immobilization, shortening of the extremity, abnormal rotation, “popping” 
sensation
○ Immediately notify the surgical team 
(Hinkle et al., 2025)

Education + Discharge
 Patient & Family Education
● Understanding of disease process and progression
● Encourage low-impact activity and gradually increase 
activities - take analgesics prior
● ***Integrative therapies: yoga, acupuncture, massage***
● Weight reduction to reduce the load on weight-bearing 
joints 
● Warm compress for stiffness, cold compress for 
inflammation
● Stair climbing can resume 3-6 weeks post-surgery 
● Sexual activity restrictions 
● Use assistive devices (canes, walkers) and address 
stigma. May not be needed once muscle tone increases 
to support normal gait without pain
● Know when to seek care: severe pain, rapid swelling, 
warmth, intense redness
Discharge & Home Care
● Total recovery takes 6+ weeks
● Promote continuity of care 
● PT/OT referral
● Supervised walking and exercise
● ADLs - Dressing: reaching device 
and long-handled shoehorns or 
tongs 
● Bathroom modifications: elevated 
toilet seat, shower chair, grab bars, 
non-slip mats
● Semi-reclining chairs 
● Fall prevention: clutter-free home, 
proper lighting & footwear
(Hinkle et al., 2025)

NCLEX Style Q&A
1. A nurse is assessing a 68-year-old client 
who has been diagnosed with osteoarthritis of 
the hands. Which finding should the nurse 
expect to see?
● A. Bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal 
joints (Heberden's nodes)
● B. Ulnar deviation with subcutaneous rheumatoid 
nodules
● C. Low-grade fever and generalized fatigue
● D. Prolonged morning stiffness lasting more than 2 
hours with symmetrical joint swelling
Correct Answer: A
Bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal joints 
(Heberden's nodes)
Rationale: Heberden's nodes (DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (PIP 
joints) are hallmark findings of osteoarthritis. Morning stiffness in OA 
typically lasts less than 30 minutes and is usually asymmetrical. 
Prolonged stiffness, systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue, ulnar 
deviation, and rheumatoid nodules are characteristic of rheumatoid 
arthritis.
2. A client with osteoarthritis of the knee is 
prescribed acetaminophen for pain 
management. Which statement by the client 
indicates that teaching about the medication 
has been effective?
● A. "I should avoid drinking alcohol while taking this 
medication."
● B. "I should take this medication only on an empty 
stomach."
● C. "This medication will reduce the inflammation in my 
joint."
● D. "I can take up to 6 grams a day if my pain is severe."
Correct Answer: A
"I should avoid drinking alcohol while taking this 
medication."
Rationale: Acetaminophen is hepatotoxic, and alcohol use increases 
the risk of liver damage. The maximum daily dose is generally 3 to 4 
grams for healthy adults (often lower for older adults or those with liver 
disease). Acetaminophen relieves pain but has little to no anti-
inflammatory effect, and it can be taken with or without food.
(Hinkle et al., 2025)
